episodes.title: THE DAVE AND JACKIE MILLER EPISODE
episodes.description:
Episode Notes — Narcissistic Abuse With Vanessa Reiser Debrief: Jackie Miller & High-Conflict Divorce
 Episode Overview Vanessa and Dave debrief their interview with Jackie Miller, a high-conflict divorce coach who brings both professional knowledge and personal experience navigating narcissistic abuse through the family court system. The conversation covers the value of divorce coaching, the dysfunction of family court, healing from narcissistic abuse, and recognizing early red flags in dating.
  
 Key Topics Covered
 1. The Value of High-Conflict Divorce Coaching
 • An estimated 96% of high-conflict divorce cases involve someone on the Cluster B personality spectrum
 • Divorce coaches like Jackie Miller can help clients strategize, control legal costs, and avoid litigation nightmares
 • Unlike attorneys and therapists, coaches are not bound by the same ethical/licensing constraints — allowing them to give raw, real, tactical advice
 • Going pro se (self-representing) can be a powerful tool to cut costs and frustrate a narcissist's attempt to bankrupt you
 2. The Family Court System
 • Family court is described as antiquated, biased, and often populated by those with their own pathological tendencies
 • Vanessa shares that she paid $40,000 in attorney fees and still didn't get the outcome she sought
 • A client of Vanessa's has faced over 2,000 motions filed against her, costing millions of dollars — the ex bankrupted himself in the process
 • The court system re-traumatizes victims and is often the narcissist's playground
 • Vanessa advises finding an attorney well-connected in your local county rather than one who claims to "understand narcissism"
 3. Understanding Narcissistic Tactics
 • Classic cycle: love bombing → idealization → devaluation → discard → hoovering
 • Narcissists will bankrupt themselves just to destroy their targets — logic does not apply
 • You cannot use logic to understand their behavior; radical acceptance is essential
 • These patterns appear not only in divorces but in corporate environments and family systems
 4. Healing from Narcissistic Abuse
 • True healing requires getting out of the abusive environment first — you cannot heal while still being re-traumatized
 • Education is approximately 80% of healing — it takes years to put all the pieces together
 • Narcissistic abuse causes measurable neurological impact, including dysregulation of the nervous system and fight/flight responses
 • Healing means reaching a point where you can discuss your experience without your nervous system being triggered
 5. Recognizing Red Flags in Dating (Post-Abuse)
 • Vanessa shares a personal dating experience: a man she had two FaceTime calls with texted "I miss you" — classic love bombing or being in a "rotation"
 • Jackie's story: a date showed up at midnight uninvited after being told no — a major boundary violation
 • Key lesson: Say "no" early and observe how someone responds to that boundary
 • Education and self-trust allow survivors to catch red flags they once would have rationalized away
 6. Covert vs. Overt Narcissists
 • Overt narcissists are often easier to spot due to grandiosity
 • Covert/vulnerable narcissists are the ones everyone loves publicly — the betrayal comes behind closed doors and is far more disorienting
  
 Quotes
 • "You have to unhand logic here. It's not showing up." — Vanessa
 • "Healing to me is getting to the point where your body starts feeling safe again." — Dave
 • "I don't think you can heal until you get the f**k out of there." — Vanessa
 • "You can't be neutral on a moving train." — Vanessa
  
 Resources Mentioned
 • Jackie Miller — high-conflict divorce coach, author, podcast host
 • Amy Palako — divorce/legal advocacy resource
 • Dr. Nadine Macaluso — therapist/advocate who gave up licensure to speak more freely
 • Dr. Ramani — narcissistic abuse educator

 In this powerful episode, Vanessa Reiser welcomes Jackie Miller, a survivor, high-conflict divorce coach, and author of Winning: Rewiring Your Brain and Reclaiming Your Life After Toxic Love. Jackie shares her personal journey through narcissistic abuse, including love bombing, boundary violations, escalating rage after pregnancy, isolation, and financial control. She explains how trauma bonds form through intermittent reinforcement and classic conditioning, the biological toll of prolonged fear on the brain, and the challenges of leaving when the abuser appears to be a "pillar of the community." Together they explore cult-like dynamics in narcissistic relationships, trusting your nervous system, reducing self-blame, and practical tools for rewiring your brain and reclaiming safety.

episodes.title: DAVE AND I UNPACK THE ANNE MARIE ALLISON EPISODE
episodes.description:
Unpacking You're Dating a Narcissist: Rom-Com, Red Flags, and Real-Life Healing
  Vanessa Reiser introduces her podcast on narcissistic abuse and, with co-host Dave, unpacks her prior interview with Anne Marie Allison, producer of the film You're Dating a Narcissist. They discuss the challenge of portraying narcissistic abuse as a rom-com while still honoring its darkness, and highlight how survivors can be trauma bonded and unable to leave due to finances, children, or culture. Vanessa shares a "hard way or hard way" framework about leaving, and they explore coercive sexual boundary-pushing as control rather than pleasure. They also cover public misconceptions about narcissism, the risks of couples therapy with abusers (including charm and therapist manipulation), and how narcissists can ruin holidays, isolate partners, and appear beloved in communities. The episode ends with a call to watch the film, build awareness, and seek support and resources.

episodes.title: THE ANNE MARIE ELLISON EPISODE
episodes.description:
You're Dating a Narcissist: Anne Marie Allison on Turning Survival into a Rom-Com
 Vanessa Reiser introduces her podcast on narcissistic abuse and welcomes writer-director-producer Anne Marie Allison, whose film You're Dating a Narcissist is inspired by a narcissistic relationship she survived in her twenties while studying psychology. Allison describes being fast-forwarded into a secret engagement, discovering extensive lying, gaslighting, and devaluation, and being helped by friends who effectively moved her into no contact, after which she was discarded. Years later, a friend's divorce and a therapist's warning helped her name the pattern, reducing shame and motivating her to write the script beginning around 2012–2013, though studios were initially confused by the topic. Reiser and Allison discuss balancing comedic tone with emotional weight, narcissistic cycles, sex as control, and the mother–daughter dynamic in the film. Allison shares that a companion book written in Judy's voice is available for preorder, and the film launches on VOD May 1, with further screenings and international sales planned.

episodes.title: THE DAVE AND EVAN RACHEL WOOD EPISODE
episodes.description:
Episode Reflections: Evan Rachel Wood on Grooming, Psychological Abuse, and Reclaiming Your Reality Narcissistic Abuse with Vanessa Reiser
  EPISODE SUMMARY In this episode of Narcissistic Abuse with Vanessa Reiser, Vanessa and co-host Dave revisit their conversation with Evan Rachel Wood, reflecting on her account of grooming, manipulation, and psychological abuse during her relationship with Marilyn Manson. Manson has denied allegations of abuse.
 Vanessa and Dave examine the behaviors Evan described, with particular attention to the calculated, forward-thinking nature of grooming. They discuss how manipulation can unfold over time, how a younger person's inexperience can be exploited, and why understanding the pattern matters more than evaluating each incident in isolation.
 A line discussed in the episode captures the conversation's focus on vulnerability and exploitation:
 "They don't trade you for somebody better. They trade you for somebody who doesn't know any better."
 The discussion explores what this means in the context of grooming, shifting attention away from a survivor's perceived shortcomings and toward the behavior of the person exploiting them.
 Vanessa and Dave also reflect on the idea that "the mask is the same underneath," considering how apparent honesty, selective vulnerability, and even moments of revealing harmful intentions can become part of a manipulative relationship. They discuss the difference between what someone presents publicly and what a partner experiences privately, including why friends, family members, and others may struggle to recognize the abuse being described.
 The conversation addresses the severity of psychological harm, including Evan's descriptions of desensitization and exposure to disturbing material. Vanessa and Dave consider how these experiences can affect a survivor's ability to trust their own perceptions and explain what happened to other people.
 They also examine a difficult question that comes up repeatedly in this work: What happens when the hope that someone will change becomes the reason a survivor keeps waiting? Vanessa and Dave discuss the risks of organizing one's safety and future around the possibility of an exception, rather than attending to the behavior occurring in the present.
 For clinicians, the episode raises questions about recognition, accountability, and education. Vanessa reflects on the tendency to make concessions for harmful behavior and the importance of helping professionals understand narcissistic abuse and coercive control rather than minimizing a survivor's experience.
 The conversation also expands beyond intimate relationships. Vanessa and Dave discuss political messaging, family influence, group loyalty, and accountability, including their comparisons between coercive relationship dynamics and larger systems of influence. These segments include discussion of Turning Point USA, youth political engagement, and the midterm elections.
 A central theme throughout the episode is the impact of speaking out. Vanessa and Dave reflect on the courage involved in Evan's public advocacy, the risks that can accompany disclosure, and their belief that survivors, clinicians, and educators can help others recognize experiences they previously struggled to name. The discussion considers both the potential value and the personal costs of telling one's story publicly.
 The episode closes with practical discussion of journaling, preserving messages, taking screenshots, and using documentation to reconnect with observable events when gaslighting creates doubt. These approaches can help some survivors validate their experiences, but documentation should always be considered alongside safety and privacy. The National Domestic Violence Hotline offers guidance on documenting abuse and storing information safely.
 At its heart, this conversation is about recognizing harmful patterns, taking psychological abuse seriously, and supporting survivors as they reclaim their sense of reality.
 KEY TOPICS DISCUSSED Grooming • Psychological abuse • Coercive control • Gaslighting • Calculated manipulation • Exploitation of youth and inexperience • Desensitization • Public image versus private behavior • Superficial charm • Apparent remorse • Projection and blame shifting • Waiting for an abusive partner to change • Survivor advocacy • The risks of speaking out • Political influence and group dynamics • Family belief systems • Clinician education • Continuing education on narcissistic abuse • Journaling and documentation • Rebuilding self-trust • Supporting survivors

episodes.title: THE EVAN RACHEL WOOD EPISODE
episodes.description:
Narcissistic Abuse with Vanessa Reiser: Evan Rachel Wood on Grooming, Coercive Control, Family Court, and Reclaiming Your Voice
   Content Warning and Disclaimer:  This episode contains discussion of alleged domestic violence, coercive control, grooming, sexual and physical abuse, substance use, trauma, PTSD, dissociation, and family court conflict. Some material may be distressing or triggering for listeners.
   This episode reflects the personal experiences, recollections, allegations, and opinions of the individuals speaking. Allegations discussed in this episode should not be interpreted as findings of fact or determinations of guilt. Brian Warner, professionally known as Marilyn Manson, has denied allegations of abuse made against him. Nothing in this podcast constitutes legal, medical, or mental health advice, and discussion of psychological concepts is for educational purposes and should not be interpreted as a clinical diagnosis of any person discussed.
   In this powerful episode of Narcissistic Abuse with Vanessa Reiser, psychotherapist and author Vanessa Reiser sits down with actor, musician, and activist Evan Rachel Wood for an in-depth conversation about grooming, coercive control, trauma, survival, advocacy, and what it can take to reclaim your voice after abuse.
   Wood discusses the abuse she has publicly alleged experiencing after meeting musician Brian Warner, known professionally as Marilyn Manson, when she was 18. She describes her recollections of grooming, isolation, psychological manipulation, escalating control, and alleged physical and sexual abuse. She also explores something survivors frequently struggle to understand: why recognizing a pattern of coercive control can be extraordinarily difficult while you are still living inside it.
   Wood and Reiser examine how abusive dynamics can develop incrementally. Their conversation explores isolation, manipulation through manufactured crises, intimidation, sleep and food disruption, temperature and environmental control, triangulation, threats, fear, intermittent reinforcement, and the erosion of a person's ability to trust their own perceptions.
   They also discuss trauma bonding and why leaving an abusive relationship is rarely as simple as "just leave." The conversation examines how fear, attachment, destabilization, substances, dissociation, and repeated cycles of distress and relief can affect a survivor's decision-making and nervous system.
   Wood describes how connecting with other women who made allegations involving Warner helped validate aspects of her own experience and gave her a new framework for understanding what had happened to her. She discusses the complicated process of speaking publicly, including her advocacy surrounding California's Phoenix Act, legislation that extended the statute of limitations for certain domestic violence offenses.
   The episode also turns to family court and post-separation abuse, including Wood's perspective on how legal proceedings can become another arena for conflict, intimidation, and control. Reiser and Wood discuss allegations of abuse by proxy, mobilizing followers or third parties, legal intimidation, and the ways survivors may continue to experience fear and destabilization long after physically leaving a relationship.
   Throughout the conversation, Wood reflects on rebuilding self-trust and learning to listen to intuition again. She discusses PTSD, dissociation, anger, survival responses, and the gradual process of helping the nervous system recognize that danger is no longer constant.
   The conversation ultimately moves beyond what happened to Wood and toward what she has chosen to do with her voice. She discusses advocacy, survival, creativity, and the freedom she found in telling her own story. For Wood, speaking publicly became part of reclaiming something that abuse had attempted to take from her: ownership of her own reality.
   Wood also shares what she is working on now, including her music project Lenore Pink, acting work, and her participation in projects examining abuse and coercive control, including Phoenix Rising and The Narcissist's Playbook.
   This is a conversation about what abuse can look like before we have language for it, why intelligent and accomplished people can become trapped in coercively controlling relationships, what happens when a survivor begins connecting the dots, and what it can mean to finally say: I believe myself.
   Please note:  Discussion of narcissism, narcissistic abuse, grooming, coercive control, trauma bonding, and related psychological concepts in this episode is intended for education and discussion. These terms should not be understood as diagnoses of any individual unless a diagnosis has been established by an appropriately qualified professional with sufficient clinical information. Vanessa Reiser is participating as a psychotherapist, educator, author, and podcast host, not as a treating clinician or forensic evaluator of the individuals discussed.
   If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence or coercive control, consider contacting a qualified local professional or domestic violence organization. In the United States, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is available at 800-799-SAFE (7233) or by texting START to 88788. If you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services.

episodes.description: EPISODE SUMMARY In this powerful solo episode, the speaker marks six years since leaving an abusive "cult of one" relationship. They share raw memories of being spit on, having clothing bleached, and receiving threats, while crediting a friend named Natalie for witnessing the abuse and helping validate reality during intense self-gaslighting. The episode offers practical advice such as recording conversations with abusive people to counter "word salad" and circular manipulation. It also explores symbolic and therapeutic outlets for healing, including running in a wedding dress to reject cultural fantasy narratives and throwing plates with names off a cliff to release anger. The speaker discusses extreme harassment by an ex, prioritizing their child's safety by encouraging him to stay with his stable father, and explains how narcissists quickly replace partners — often targeting those who "don't know any better" or viewing strong people as "sport." The episode emphasizes that the abuse is never about the victim and encourages becoming "ungroomable" through strong boundaries, stable finances, supportive friends, hobbies, and a solid career. Healing is framed as rebellion, and peace as revolution. episodes.title: THE EMMA DAVEY EPISODE
episodes.description:
Surviving Coercive Control: Emma Davey on Narcissistic Abuse, Evidence, Justice, and Recovery

Narcissistic Abuse with Vanessa Reiser

EPISODE SUMMARY

In this powerful episode, Vanessa Reiser sits down with Emma Davey, founder of My Trauma Therapy and creator of the MyNARA narcissistic abuse recovery app, to discuss Emma’s journey from coercive control and narcissistic abuse to survival, justice, and helping others heal.

Emma shares how, at 26, she entered a fast-moving relationship in 2015 with a 49-year-old man. What began with intense love bombing and future-faking gradually transformed into isolation and escalating coercive control. Her partner began controlling her clothing, finances, access to her car, and ultimately her sense of identity. The relationship progressed into severe psychological and physical abuse, contributing to self-harm and suicide attempts.

At her breaking point, Emma fled to Australia with the help of a friend. That physical distance gave her the safety and clarity to begin understanding what had happened to her. She discovered the language of narcissistic abuse and coercive control, trained as a counselor, became a certified narcissistic abuse specialist, and eventually returned to the UK.

Emma also did something that would become critically important: she preserved the evidence.

Texts. Voice notes. Threats. Communications. Patterns of behavior.

Despite initially feeling dismissed by police, Emma continued documenting what was happening. In 2022, her abuser was ultimately convicted of coercive control, sentenced to 19 months in prison, and given a restraining order.

Emma discusses the realities of trauma bonding, post-separation stalking, the public charm that can mask abuse, why survivors stay, and why leaving can be one of the most dangerous periods in an abusive relationship.

The conversation also addresses non-fatal strangulation as a serious warning sign, particularly because strangulation can be minimized or normalized despite its association with potentially lethal violence. Emma shares that her former abuser was subsequently convicted of non-fatal strangulation involving another victim.

Today, Emma has transformed her experience into advocacy and clinical work. In addition to supporting survivors, she is conducting master’s research examining adolescents’ understanding of coercive control, with the goal of helping younger generations recognize abusive relationship patterns before they become entrenched.

This is a conversation about what coercive control actually looks like behind closed doors, why believing survivors matters, the importance of preserving evidence, and what it can take to reclaim your life after narcissistic abuse.

KEY TOPICS DISCUSSED

Love bombing and future-faking • Coercive control • Isolation • Financial abuse • Control over clothing and identity • Alcohol and the abuse cycle • Trauma bonding • Self-harm and suicidal crisis • Escaping an abusive relationship • Post-separation stalking • Preserving evidence • Police response • Criminal prosecution • Public charm and the narcissistic mask • Anchoring and nicknames • Recognizing danger through pets • Covert narcissistic abuse • Safety after leaving • Trauma therapy • Healing and rebuilding identity • Non-fatal strangulation • Femicide risk • Teaching adolescents about coercive control
